section.title: The Transfiguration
section.sectionRationale: Six days after the confession and the first passion prediction, Jesus is unveiled in glory on the mountain, with the Father's own voice confirming Peter's confession. Then comes the descent into a world of unbelief, a failed exorcism, a second passion prediction, and a quiet lesson about the temple tax.
section.thesis: On the mountain the Father unveils the glory of His beloved Son and commands, Listen to Him, confirming that the suffering Christ is the radiant Lord; and back in the valley that same Son heals what faithless disciples cannot, foretells His death again, and shows Himself the Son who is free yet stoops to pay.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the transfiguration and the Father's voice; the coming of Elijah in John the Baptist; the boy with a demon and the power of faith; the second passion prediction; and the temple tax.

verses.text: After six days Jesus took with Him Peter, James, and John the brother of James, and led them up a high mountain by themselves.
There He was {{metamorphoo|transfigured}} before them. His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as the light.
Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared before them, talking with Jesus.
Peter said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If You wish, I will put up three shelters, one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”
While Peter was still speaking, a bright cloud enveloped them, and a voice from the cloud said, “This is My {{agapetos|beloved}} Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!”
When the disciples heard this, they fell facedown in terror.
Then Jesus came over and touched them. “Get up,” He said. “Do not be afraid.”
And when they looked up, they saw no one except Jesus.
As they were coming down the mountain, Jesus commanded them, “Do not tell anyone about this vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead.”
The disciples asked Him, “Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”
Jesus replied, “Elijah does indeed come, and he will restore all things.
But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but have done to him whatever they wished. In the same way, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.”
Then the disciples understood that He was speaking to them about John the Baptist.
When they came to the crowd, a man came up to Jesus and knelt before Him.
“Lord, have mercy on my son,” he said. “He has seizures and is suffering terribly. He often falls into the fire or into the water.
I brought him to Your disciples, but they could not heal him.”
“O unbelieving and perverse generation!” Jesus replied. “How long must I remain with you? How long must I put up with you? Bring the boy here to Me.”
Then Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of the boy, and he was healed from that moment.
Afterward the disciples came to Jesus privately and asked, “Why couldn’t we drive it out?”

“Because you have so little faith,” He answered. “For truly I tell you, if you have {{pistis|faith}} the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move. Nothing will be impossible for you.”
When they gathered together in Galilee, Jesus told them, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.
They will kill Him, and on the third day He will be raised to life.” And the disciples were deeply grieved.

units.label: The temple tax
units.note: the free Son who stoops to pay

verses.text: After they had arrived in Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax came to Peter and asked, “Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?”

“Yes,” he answered. When Peter entered the house, Jesus preempted him. “What do you think, Simon?” He asked. “From whom do the kings of the earth collect customs and taxes: from their own sons, or from others?”
“From others,” Peter answered. “Then the sons are exempt,” Jesus said to him.

“But so that we may not offend them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish you catch. When you open its mouth, you will find a four-drachma coin. Take it and give it to them for My tax and yours.”

metamorphoo.gloss: To be transformed, changed in form; the source of the word metamorphosis. On the mountain Jesus' hidden glory shines through His humanity, a momentary unveiling of who He truly is. The same verb describes the believer's inner transformation, Romans 12:2, 2 Corinthians 3:18.

agapetos.gloss: Beloved, dearly loved. The Father's word from the cloud, My beloved Son, echoes the baptism and marks Jesus as the unique, cherished Son to whom all must listen.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust in God. Even faith as small as a mustard seed, if it is real reliance on God's power, accomplishes what is humanly impossible; the disciples failed not for lack of technique but for lack of faith.

basic.context: Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain and is transfigured, His face shining like the sun. Moses and Elijah appear, and the Father's voice declares, This is My beloved Son; listen to Him. Coming down, Jesus explains that Elijah has already come in John the Baptist. He heals a boy the disciples could not, teaching that even mustard-seed faith moves mountains. He foretells His death a second time, and He provides the temple tax from a fish's mouth.
basic.hermeneutics: The transfiguration confirms Peter's confession and frames the whole road to the cross: the suffering Son is also the radiant Lord. Moses and Elijah, the Law and the Prophets, point to Him and then withdraw so only Jesus remains. The valley scenes show what discipleship needs, faith, and who Jesus is, the free Son of the King who still stoops.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus is metamorphoo, transfigured, His glory shining out. The Father names Him agapetos, beloved. And the disciples fail for want of pistis, faith, which even mustard-seed small can move mountains.
basic.typology: The shining face recalls Moses on Sinai; the mountain, the cloud, and the voice recall God's presence at Sinai. Jesus is the prophet like Moses to whom Israel must listen. Moses and Elijah, who both met God on a mountain, now meet the One they foretold.
basic.christ: Jesus is the beloved Son, radiant with divine glory, greater than Moses and Elijah, the one to whom the Law and the Prophets give way. He is the suffering Son of Man and the exempt Son of the King who still pays the tax, humble and free at once.
basic.god: The Father speaks from the cloud, confirming and commanding: this is My Son, listen to Him. God unveils glory to strengthen faith for the coming suffering, and He meets terror with the tender word through Jesus, do not be afraid.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 24 and 34 give the mountain, cloud, and shining face. Deuteronomy 18 promises a prophet like Moses to whom Israel must listen. Malachi 4 promises Elijah before the day of the Lord. 2 Peter 1 recalls the majesty on the holy mountain.
basic.oneStory: At the hinge of the Gospel, the Father unveils the glory of the beloved Son and commands the world to listen to Him. The suffering foretold in the previous chapter is set against the shining truth of who Jesus is. Then He descends into a faithless world to heal, to foretell His death again, and to pay a tax He does not owe, the glorious Son walking the humble road to the cross.

context.literary:
Matthew 17 is built as a mountain scene flanked by valley scenes, and the hinge between them is the sentence in verse 9 about being raised from the dead. Before the hinge, glory; after it, a boy thrown into fire and water, a second announcement of death, and a coin in a fish's mouth. The chapter is a diptych on one theme, that the Son of God is seen most truly where He is also most willing to be lowered. The opening words, after six days, tie the scene back to Matthew 16:21-28, where Jesus first spoke of the cross and promised that some standing there would see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom, Matthew 16:28. That promise is the immediate frame for what follows.

Within the mountain scene the movement is sight, then sound, then touch. The disciples see the change in verse 2, hear the voice in verse 5, and are touched and raised in verse 7. Matthew twice marks the shift with the word idou, behold or suddenly, in verses 3 and 5, so that each new element breaks in on Peter, who is still talking. The scene ends on the single most important sentence in the paragraph, that they saw no one except Jesus, verse 8. Everything before it is stripped away and one figure is left.

The descent mirrors the ascent. The disciples who went up with Jesus come down into a crowd and a failure. Matthew arranges three requests for explanation, the scribes and Elijah in verse 10, the disciples' private question in verse 19, and Peter's embarrassed yes in verse 25, each answered by Jesus out of a knowledge the asker did not have. Two brief passion announcements, 17:9 and 17:22-23, stand like pillars on either side of the healing, and the temple tax closes the chapter with a small, almost comic act that carries a very large claim about who Jesus is.
context.historical:
Jewish hearers would have recognised the scene's furniture at once. A high mountain, a cloud, a shining face and a voice were the equipment of Sinai, Exodus 24:15-18 and 34:29-35. The cloud was the sign that God Himself was present, and Israel had learned to hold it with awe. The six days of verse 1 even follow Exodus 24:16, where the cloud covered Sinai for six days and God called Moses on the seventh. The setting also fits the season of feasts. Peter's offer to build shelters naturally calls to mind the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles, Leviticus 23:42-43, a festival that looked back to the wilderness and forward to God dwelling among His people.

Moses and Elijah were the two figures of Israel's memory who had stood on Horeb and met God there. Moses received the law on Sinai and Elijah ran there in despair, 1 Kings 19:8-13. Both had strange ends: Moses was buried by God, Deuteronomy 34:6, and Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind, 2 Kings 2:11. The expectation of Elijah's return before the day of the LORD, Malachi 4:5, was current teaching among the scribes, which is why the disciples ask the question of verse 10.

The tax scene is also precise. The collectors of the two-drachma tax were collecting the half-shekel that Exodus 30:11-16 required of each man for the service of the Tent of Meeting, a ransom or atonement payment, later treated as an annual temple levy. Nehemiah 10:32 shows the amount being adjusted in the exile. A stater was a silver coin worth approximately one shekel, as the BSB footnote says, which is why one coin covers two men. The setting is Capernaum, the town Matthew calls Jesus' own city, so the collectors come to the man in whose house the Teacher lives, Peter.
context.canonical:
The transfiguration is the fullest echo of Sinai in the Gospels, and it is quoted by name in the New Testament. Peter writes that he was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty and heard the voice come from the Majestic Glory on the holy mountain, 2 Peter 1:16-18, using this scene to anchor the apostolic message in something seen and heard rather than in clever stories. John's Gospel does not narrate the scene, but his words about seeing glory, John 1:14, are widely heard as its echo.

The voice itself is a weaving of three Old Testament lines. You are My Son recalls Psalm 2:7, the royal decree of the anointed King. In whom I am well pleased recalls Isaiah 42:1, the chosen Servant on whom God puts His Spirit. The word beloved son is the language God used to Abraham about Isaac, Genesis 22:2, a father asked to give up a son on a mountain. The command to listen answers Deuteronomy 18:15, the promise of a prophet like Moses. In one sentence the Father names the King, the Servant, the sacrificial Son and the new prophet.

The shining face looks forward as well as back. The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, Matthew 13:43, and Daniel 12:3 says the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens. Paul says believers will be transformed to be like His glorious body, Philippians 3:21, and uses the same verb that Matthew uses for Jesus when he says we are being transformed into the Lord's image, 2 Corinthians 3:18. The scene is a preview, offered to three men, of what the redeemed will one day be.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wrote for a community that knew the shape of the Law and the Prophets and needed to hear that both converge on Jesus. The six days link, the sun-bright face and the voice are meant to be read together as God's own commentary on Peter's confession in Matthew 16:16. A church that would face rejection needed to know that the man who was about to be handed over was the Son whom God had named. Matthew also means this scene to explain why the disciples' later failure and grief do not cancel their calling: they had seen, and they were told to keep silent only until the resurrection, verse 9.

The valley scenes are not an anticlimax. Matthew wants his readers to feel the contrast between the glory the three have just seen and the helplessness of the nine at the foot of the mountain. The disciples have power as sent ones, Matthew 10:1, yet are powerless here, and Jesus names the cause as faith. The temple tax then puts a very small question to a very large claim: if Jesus is the Son, the sons of the King are free, and yet He chooses to pay. Matthew wants readers who are citizens of the kingdom to carry that same freedom with the same gentleness toward the world around them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this chapter records what happened to specific people at a specific moment. No one is told to seek a mountaintop vision, and Peter's wish to stay on the mountain is gently set aside, not held up as a model. The experience is unrepeated and belongs to the three witnesses, which is why Jesus restricts it until the resurrection.

The prescriptions are few and clear. The Father's one command is to listen to the Son, verse 5, and that applies to every reader. Jesus' touch and His word do not be afraid, verse 7, are given as a pattern of how He meets the terrified. The teaching on faith is prescriptive in its direction though not in a formula: faith that is small but real, directed at God's power, is enough. The tax scene is a case of judgment, not a rule to pay every demand. Jesus pays so as not to cause offence, using the very verb he warns about in Matthew 18:6, and He does so by His own provision, not by compromising who He is.

debates.question: Why do Moses and Elijah appear?

views.label: The Law and the Prophets as witnesses
views.case: Moses stands for the Law and Elijah for the Prophets, and together they confirm the testimony of the whole Old Testament to Jesus, in line with the rule that a matter is established by two or three witnesses, Deuteronomy 19:15. Matthew then narrows the scene to Jesus alone, verse 8, and the Father's command to listen to Him.

views.label: Prophets who suffered and were vindicated
views.case: Both men were rejected by Israel in their day, and both left the earth in unusual ways. On this view their presence anticipates the suffering of the Son of Man, which Luke makes explicit when he says they spoke of His departure to be accomplished at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31.

views.label: Figures of the last days
views.case: Malachi 4:4-5 pairs the law of Moses with the coming of Elijah, and Jewish expectation looked for both in the last days. Their presence marks the long-awaited time as arrived.

debates.bearing: These views are not rivals. Moses and Elijah witness to Jesus from the Law and the Prophets, share His pattern of rejection and vindication, and mark the arrival of the age they were waiting for. Matthew's own stress is on the way they step aside so that Jesus alone remains.

debates.question: Was Peter wrong to propose building shelters?

views.label: A well meant but mistaken offer
views.case: Luke adds that Peter did not know what he was saying, Luke 9:33, and the Father's voice interrupts him while he is still speaking. On this view the offer treats Jesus as one of three equals and tries to freeze the glory before the cross.

views.label: An instinct drawn from the Feast of Tabernacles
views.case: Booths belonged to the festival remembering God's dwelling with Israel, and Peter's instinct is to keep the meeting going. The error is not the desire for the presence but the timing and the equal footing of three tents.

debates.bearing: The Father's reply settles the matter. Peter is not told to stop worshipping but to listen, and the disciples find that the glory they wanted to hold is only held in the Son who walks down the mountain toward Jerusalem.

debates.question: Is the transfiguration the fulfilment of Matthew 16:28?

views.label: Yes, a preview of the coming kingdom
views.case: The scene follows the promise by six days and shows three men the Son of Man in glory, as the promise said some would see. Peter's later use of the scene as a witness to the power and coming of Christ, 2 Peter 1:16, supports the link.

views.label: A larger fulfilment through the resurrection and the church
views.case: Others read the saying as reaching beyond one mountain to the resurrection, Pentecost and the spread of the kingdom, with the transfiguration as the first foretaste.

debates.bearing: Whichever way the saying is read, the transfiguration belongs inside it. It is the first time the Son of Man is seen coming in His kingdom's glory, and it prepares for what the cross and the empty tomb will unveil.

debates.question: In what sense had Elijah already come?

views.label: Fulfilled in John the Baptist
views.case: Jesus says Elijah has already come and was not recognised, and Matthew adds that the disciples understood He meant John the Baptist, verse 13. This fits Jesus' earlier words about John in Matthew 11:14, where He says that if you are willing to accept it, John is the Elijah who was to come.

views.label: A further restoration still awaited
views.case: Jesus also says Elijah does come and will restore all things, verse 11, which some take to leave room for a fuller end time fulfilment beyond John, alongside the fulfilment already given.

debates.bearing: The plain sense is that John fulfils the Elijah promise. Whether one also expects a further restoration, the point is the same: the forerunner was rejected, and the Son of Man will suffer in the same way.

study.originalLanguages:
Matthew's verb for the change in verse 2 is metamorphoo, to change form. It is a passive, so the change is something that happens to Jesus rather than something He does, and the voice that follows is the Father's interpretation of it. The word is rare in the New Testament. Paul uses it for believers who are transformed by the renewing of the mind, Romans 12:2, and for those who are being changed into the Lord's likeness from one degree of glory to another, 2 Corinthians 3:18. The same Greek verb stands behind Jesus' unveiling and the believer's slow transformation, so that the mountain is a picture of the road the disciples themselves are on.

The word translated bright in the phrase a bright cloud is the Greek adjective for light, and Matthew uses light words for the face and the clothes as well. He says the face shone like the sun, and the clothes became as white as the light. The sun comparison belongs to Matthew alone among the Synoptics and is the same comparison used of the righteous in Matthew 13:43 and of the risen Christ in Revelation 1:16.

The command listen to Him is a present imperative, akouete, which in Greek suggests continuing, habitual hearing and not a single act. The verb's object stands in the genitive, the case that fits attentive listening rather than merely hearing sounds. The disciples are told to go on listening to this Son, which fits the context at once: they are about to hear what they do not want to hear, that He must be delivered and killed, verse 22.

The simple sentence Get up, in verse 7, uses the verb egeiro, the same verb that Jesus uses a few verses later for the Son of Man being raised from the dead, verse 9, and again for His being raised on the third day, verse 23. Matthew has Jesus say to frightened men on the ground the very word the Gospel will use at the empty tomb, Matthew 28:6.

In the valley the father says the boy has seizures. The Greek verb is seleniazomai, built on the word for moon, and Matthew uses it also in Matthew 4:24. Matthew separates it from demon possession in Matthew 4:24 but here joins the two, since Jesus rebukes a demon and the boy is healed.

Jesus says the generation is unbelieving and perverse, apistos and diestrammene, and the second word is a perfect passive participle meaning twisted. It echoes Deuteronomy 32:5 and 32:20, where Moses calls Israel a perverse and crooked generation, so Jesus sounds like a new Moses coming down a mountain to find a people that has gone wrong.

Last, the tax scene uses a verb the reader has already met. The word offend in verse 27 is skandalizo, the verb of Matthew 18:6 for causing little ones to stumble. The free Son pays so as not to cause a stumbling block.

typology.type: Moses coming down from Sinai with a shining face, Exodus 34:29-35
typology.fulfillment: Moses descended with a face radiant from speaking with the LORD, and the people feared to approach him, Exodus 34:29-30. Jesus' face shines not with light received but with His own, and He touches the terrified and tells them not to be afraid. Paul draws the contrast in 2 Corinthians 3:7-18: the glory on Moses was fading and veiled, while the glory in Christ is unveiled and transforms those who look at Him. The type falls short because Moses covered his face to shield the people, whereas Jesus draws His disciples close.

Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like himself, and Israel was told to listen. The Father's command on the mountain, listen to Him, picks up that very word. Jesus is greater than Moses in the way a son is greater than a servant, Hebrews 3:5-6. Peter in Acts 3:22 and Stephen in Acts 7:37 both apply the promise to Him. The correspondence holds for the work of speaking God's word, but it breaks at the point of identity: Moses was a servant in God's house and Jesus is the Son over it.

typology.type: Elijah who goes before the day of the LORD, Malachi 4:5-6
typology.fulfillment: Malachi promised that Elijah would come to turn hearts before the great day. Jesus says that Elijah has come in John the Baptist, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah, Luke 1:17. John did not restore all things by himself, and it is Christ who brings the restoring that Elijah's work prepared for. The type falls short in that John was a forerunner who ended in prison and death, while the One he announced reigns. Jesus ties the forerunner's fate to His own, saying the Son of Man will suffer in the same way, verse 12.

typology.type: The booths of the wilderness and the shelters Peter offers, Leviticus 23:42-43
typology.fulfillment: Israel lived in booths to remember that God brought them out of Egypt and dwelt with them. Peter's offer expresses the same longing to keep God close. John writes that the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us, John 1:14, a verb related to the Greek word for tent. The fulfilment is that God does not need a booth built for Him on a mountain because He has pitched His tent in a human life. Revelation 21:3 carries the same promise to its end: the dwelling of God is with men.

typology.type: The half shekel as a ransom for life, Exodus 30:11-16
typology.fulfillment: The half shekel was paid by every man, rich and poor alike, as an offering to atone for his life and serve the Tent of Meeting. Jesus, the Son, pays it with a coin He provides, not by owing it. The pattern prepares for Matthew 20:28, where He gives His own life as a ransom for many. The type points forward but falls short: the half shekel covered the service of a sanctuary for a year, and Christ's single offering secures the redemption once for all, Hebrews 9:12.

study.christ:
The transfiguration confirms Peter's confession by the Father's own word, and the key is the order of what Matthew records. Peter had said you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, Matthew 16:16, and Jesus had answered with the cross. Six days later the Father agrees with the first and sets the glory beside the second. Matthew does not set glory against suffering. The same Jesus is both, and the Father's voice names Him as the Son at the very moment He is about to walk toward being delivered.

Jesus is the new and greater Moses. The shining face, the cloud and the voice are Sinai, but here the One in the centre is not the mediator receiving a law; He is the Son the law pointed to. Moses and Elijah talk with Him and then are gone, verse 8. The Law and the Prophets are not cancelled but handed over, since Jesus says elsewhere that He came to fulfil them, Matthew 5:17. Hebrews begins by saying that God spoke long ago by the prophets and has spoken in these last days by His Son, Hebrews 1:1-2, and the mountain is a picture of that sentence.

He is also the Servant and the sacrificial Son of the voice. The words in whom I am well pleased draw on Isaiah 42:1, which the Gospel has already used at the baptism in Matthew 3:17 and in Matthew 12:18. The word beloved recalls the father who was told to take his beloved son up a mountain, Genesis 22:2. In Isaiah 53:10 it was the LORD's will to crush the Servant, and the Father who says well pleased on the mountain is the Father who will not spare His own Son, Romans 8:32.

The valley shows His authority and His patience. He rebukes the demon with a word, and the boy is healed from that moment. He also names the disciples' failure as little faith, and His cry how long must I remain with you is not rage but the weariness of a Son who has come from heaven to a people who still do not trust, Deuteronomy 32:5.

The two final scenes turn on the same hinge. In the second announcement the Son of Man is about to be delivered, and in the temple tax the free Son stoops. These are one gesture. He who is exempt pays, and He who is glorious will be handed over. Paul says that though He was rich, yet for our sake He became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and Philippians 2:6-8 says the same in the language of a servant.

Care is needed here not to turn every detail into a coded picture. The fish and the coin are not allegories, and the stater is not a symbol of anything else. They show Jesus' knowledge and His provision, and they put a small act of humility beside a very large claim.
study.god:
The Father speaks, and what He says is the doctrine of God in miniature. He speaks as the Father of the Son, as the One who is pleased, and as the One who commands. The statement about delight shows that the Father's love for the Son is not a recent fact. It is the settled ground of everything He does. The word listen shows that the God of Israel does not remain silent behind Moses and Elijah. He speaks again, and He speaks through a Person.

The cloud tells us how God is present. In the Old Testament the cloud both revealed and hid, and Israel could not see God and live, Exodus 33:20. Here the cloud overshadows the disciples, but when it clears they see Jesus only, verse 8. God is present in a way that does not destroy them, because the Son stands among them in the flesh. The terror of verse 6 is the right response to holiness, as Daniel and Isaiah were undone before the divine glory, Daniel 10:9 and Isaiah 6:5, and the touch of verse 7 is the gospel's answer to it.

The scene holds together two things that often seem to compete. God is utterly glorious and God is gentle. The same Lord whose face shines like the sun stoops, touches, and says do not be afraid. In the same way, God is absolutely free and sovereign, and yet He submits to the ordinary obligations of His people. The temple tax is paid from a coin God provides, so that even in condescension God remains the one who supplies.

The scene also shows God's patience and His plan. He gives the disciples a glimpse of glory before they hear that the Son will be killed, so that the shock of the cross will not be the end of what they know. God does not hide the suffering from His people, and He does not leave them with the suffering alone. He tells them it comes, and that it will be followed by raising.

For worship, the scene teaches the posture of the disciples in order. They fall down, they are raised by the Son's touch, and they follow Him down the mountain. Worship is not an attempt to hold on to an experience; it is hearing, trusting and following. The command to listen makes every Christian assembly, whatever else it includes, a place where the Son is heard.

crossReferences.note: The six days, the cloud and the glory on the mountain at Sinai. Matthew's opening words, after six days, and the cloud that covers the three disciples put the transfiguration in the line of this meeting between God and Moses, with Jesus now at the centre of the scene.

Moses' face was radiant from speaking with the LORD, and the people feared to approach. Jesus' face shines in His own right, and He draws near to the terrified disciples and touches them. Paul picks up this story in 2 Corinthians 3 to contrast fading glory with the glory of Christ.

The promise of a prophet like Moses, with the command You must listen to him. The Father's final words from the cloud take up that very command and apply it to Jesus, setting the Son over every earlier voice.

The promise of Elijah before the great and awesome Day of the LORD. Jesus applies it to John the Baptist and says the disciples understood, so the closing words of the Old Testament are answered in the forerunner's ministry.

The royal decree You are My Son. The Father's words from the cloud and at the baptism in Matthew 3:17 gather this royal sonship together with the Servant of Isaiah 42:1, showing Jesus as King and Servant in one person.

Abraham was told to take his beloved son up a mountain. The voice's phrase beloved Son recalls this account, and the Father who will not withhold His own Son, Romans 8:32, stands behind the mountain of Matthew 17.

Peter looks back on this very scene as an eyewitness. He says the apostles did not follow cleverly devised fables but saw the majesty and heard the voice, so the transfiguration becomes part of the apostolic evidence for the power and coming of the Lord.

Luke's parallel adds that Moses and Elijah spoke of His departure, the Greek word being exodus, about to be accomplished at Jerusalem. He also says the disciples were heavy with sleep. The detail ties the glory to the road to the cross.

The promise that some standing there would see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom before tasting death. The transfiguration follows by six days, and the two passages belong together as promise and its first preview.

The half shekel for the service of the Tent of Meeting, the root of the two-drachma tax in verse 24. Reading it shows that the tax carried the idea of a ransom for life, and that the free Son's payment sits near the theme of Matthew 20:28.

Moses calls Israel a perverse and crooked generation. Jesus' cry, O unbelieving and perverse generation, uses language from this song, making Him the new Moses meeting a people who have again turned aside.

The verb used for causing little ones to stumble is the same one Jesus uses for offending the tax collectors in 17:27. The next chapter's stern warning about stumbling is already at work in the free Son's care not to cause offence.

study.oneStory:
The story begins in the garden with a God who walks with His people and a command to rule and fill the earth. After the fall the glory recedes and the presence is hidden behind a veil, a cloud and a mountain. Sinai, Exodus 24 and 34, is the high point of the old arrangement: a mountain that cannot be touched, a cloud that terrifies, a mediator whose face must be veiled. Transfiguration is where the whole structure is shown to be a promise. The cloud comes again and the face shines again, but this time the glory is the glory of a human being who stands among the disciples and puts His hand on them.

The scene answers the question the Old Testament keeps asking: when will God speak again, and will it be possible to bear it? It says that He speaks through His Son, and that those who fall down are raised. It answers the question Elijah's promise raised, whether the forerunner will come, with the answer yes, and he has been and was rejected. It also takes the pattern of Israel's long exile from the presence and turns it, for a moment, into homecoming.

It sets up what comes next. The same chapter that shows the glory announces the cross, and the three disciples who see the glory will also be the three who see the agony in Gethsemane, Matthew 26:37. The glory they saw on the mountain is the glory that the cross will not extinguish but purchase for all who belong to Him. After the resurrection the disciples will go to another mountain in Galilee, where Jesus says all authority has been given Him and sends them to the nations, Matthew 28:16-20, and the command to listen becomes the command to go and teach.

The story ends where the transfiguration points. John sees the One whose face is like the sun shining in full strength, Revelation 1:16, and the redeemed shine like the sun, Matthew 13:43. In the new Jerusalem there is no need of sun, because the glory of God gives it light and its lamp is the Lamb, Revelation 21:23. What three men saw for a moment on the mountain is the permanent light of the new creation, where the cloud no longer hides and the whole company of God's people looks at the face of the Son.

quiz.q: What did the Father's voice from the cloud declare?

options.text: This is My beloved Son; listen to Him, confirming Jesus' glory and authority.
options.note: Verse 5 gives the Father's affirmation and command.

options.text: That Jesus was a great prophet like Moses and Elijah.
options.note: Jesus is the prophet like Moses, but the voice sets Him above them as the beloved Son, not merely alongside them.

options.text: That the disciples should build three shelters on the mountain.
options.note: That was Peter's suggestion, which the voice effectively overrides by pointing only to the Son.

options.text: That Moses and Elijah were equal to Jesus.
options.note: They withdraw so that only Jesus remains; He is the beloved Son to be heard.

quiz.q: Why did Moses and Elijah appear, and then only Jesus remained?

options.text: The Law and the Prophets bear witness to Jesus and then give way to Him alone.
options.note: Their appearing and withdrawing show all Scripture pointing to the Son, seen alone in verse 8.

options.text: To show that Jesus stood in the line of Israel's great leaders.
options.note: He fulfills that line, but the scene shows Him surpassing it, not merely joining it.

options.text: To give the disciples three teachers to follow equally.
options.note: The Father commands them to listen to the Son, not to three equal voices.

options.text: To prove that Moses and Elijah had never really died.
options.note: The point is Jesus' glory and supremacy, not speculation about the two prophets.

quiz.q: Why could the disciples not drive out the demon?

options.text: Because of their little faith; real reliance on God's power was lacking.
options.note: Verse 20 names their little faith as the cause.

options.text: Because the demon was an unusually powerful kind.
options.note: The difficulty was real, but Jesus locates the failure in their faith, not the demon's strength.

options.text: Because they had not been given authority to cast out demons.
options.note: They had been given such authority in chapter 10; the issue was faith, not authorization.

options.text: Because Jesus alone could ever cast out demons.
options.note: Jesus expected them to, and taught that faith like a mustard seed would suffice.

quiz.q: What does the temple tax episode reveal about Jesus?

options.text: As the Son of the King He is exempt, yet He freely stoops to pay so as not to give offense.
options.note: Verses 25-27 show His freedom as the Son and His gracious submission.

options.text: That Jesus always obeyed every tax law without exception.
options.note: He does pay, but the point is His freedom as the Son who chooses to pay, not mere law-keeping.

options.text: That Jesus was subject to the temple like everyone else.
options.note: He declares the sons exempt; He pays by gracious choice, not obligation.

options.text: That Jesus refused to pay the temple tax.
options.note: He pays it, providing the coin from the fish's mouth.

questions: The Father commands, listen to Him. Whose voices are competing for your attention, and what would it mean to truly listen to Jesus this week?
The glory of Christ was given to steady the disciples before suffering. How does a fresh sight of who Jesus is strengthen you for what you are facing?
Jesus traced the disciples' failure to little faith. Where are you relying on your own technique or effort instead of trusting God's power?
The radiant Son came down into a faithless valley to heal. How does it encourage you that His glory does not keep Him from your mess and need?
The free Son chose to pay rather than give needless offense. Where might love lead you to yield a right you could rightfully claim?

translationNotes.note: The BSB numbering goes from verse 20 to verse 22; verse 21, this kind does not come out except by prayer and fasting, is not included in the earliest manuscripts and appears as a footnote drawn from Mark 9:29.
The two-drachma tax is the annual half-shekel temple tax of Exodus 30:13; the coin found in the fish is a stater, a four-drachma piece worth about a shekel, enough for both Jesus and Peter.
